content.thinking:
I'm figuring out realistic proportions for a pixel-art monster truck—roughly 5.5m long, 3.6m wide and tall with giant 66-inch tires—and thinking through what texel scale and texture resolution would work for the model.

Reconsidering the proportions, in real monster trucks the tires sit mostly outboard of the narrower body, with the fenders cut away. I'll set the tire track centers at ±1.45 m with tire width 1.0 m, giving inner faces at 0.95 and outer at 1.95, while the body itself is narrower, around 2.0 m wide, sitting above and between the tire inner edges with its bottom around y=1.3.

Now I'm thinking through the wheel joints and tire geometry — lathing a cylindrical tire profile for tread, then adding staggered lug blocks around the circumference, merging them per wheel to keep part count manageable (one part per bone and color).

Switching to a cylinder geometry for the tire core instead, rotated so its axis aligns with x. For the wheel joint I'll build the geometry at the origin in local space—rotating the cylinder and positioning lugs around the axis by angle—then merge everything and translate the whole assembly to the hub position afterward.

Now I'm working out the rim and hub details: a silver disc with lug nuts and a red hub cap, all facing outward along x. For the sidewall, I'm considering adding pixel-art lettering or a painted ring pattern using a radial distance check against the face normal, rather than trying to render real text.

I'm thinking I could define a tiny pixel font to spell out a truck name like "MUD HOG" across the sidewall or door decal, using a simple 3x5 grid for each letter.

Settling on a flame-orange body with yellow flame decals, black roof stripe, steel-blue-grey chassis, and chrome details for a classic monster-truck palette. Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy starting from the chassis root and working outward to the wheels.

Planning the suspension and steering rig: front wheels get steer joints at the hubs with hinge rotation feeding into wheel spin joints, while axle beams, differentials, and shock components attach as rigid approximations between the chassis and axles. I'm also adding hinge joints for the doors, hood, and tailgate so they can open.

For extra detail, I'm considering a driver silhouette visible through the cab glass, plus small touches like an antenna flag and exhaust stacks to round out the model, keeping most of these as static rigid parts rather than articulated joints to avoid over-complicating the rig.

I'm deciding to skip self-lit glow effects for headlights and taillights, opting instead for simple bright flat colors to stay true to the pixel-art style, and planning out the body shell as blocky boxes with tiled paint textures to simulate panel shading.

For texturing I'm weighing tileBox versus cellPaint — tileBox repeats the same crop on every face so getting consistent shading across different box sizes requires carefully scaling the tile dimensions, whereas cellPaint works in world-space with dithering based on surface normal, which would give more uniform top-lit shading across the whole truck regardless of box size.

Decals like flames can be painted procedurally with cellPaint by computing height functions along side faces to produce zigzag flame tongues with layered yellow/orange coloring. I'm estimating texel density for the paint sheet — roughly 80m² of surface at 1024px gives about 1cm per texel, with 4 texels per 0.04m cell, and considering bumping to 2048 for sharper detail without blowing past the atlas limit.

Now I'm planning the truck body: frame rails as axis-aligned boxes spanning z=-2.3 to 2.3 with cross members, axles positioned at hub height with tire radius 0.85m, and axle tubes sized with appropriate radius between the wheel hubs. Flat colors stay under the 64-color limit since paints don't count toward that, so large surfaces use paint and small details use flat colors.

I'm figuring out the suspension geometry — placing shock towers and coilovers between the axles and chassis rails, keeping things simple with angled shocks near the tires rather than full realism, since body panels would otherwise clip through the hardware.

I'm positioning the shocks so they stand visible just in front of the tire's inner side, mounted on towers running from the axle up to a higher point, placing them between the body's wheel arch corner and the tire.

Now I'm checking the frame bracket beam connecting the chassis rail out to the shock tower, keeping it tucked under the body floor so it doesn't poke through, before adding a vertical post up to the tower.

I'm figuring out the overall height stack-up: hub center, body floor, cab roof, trying to match proportions of a real monster truck (around 3.6 m tall with roll bar) against a pickup body sitting on the frame.

Adding the antenna brings total height to about 3.3, which works. I'm placing the chassis rails and body floor pan so there's a visible gap underneath, checking that the wheel arches clear the tire tops properly, and now I'm working out the pickup body's length and z-range along with the wheelbase proportions.

Settling on roughly a 3.0m wheelbase matching real monster truck specs, I'm checking that the front tire span leaves enough overhang for the body front edge, then breaking the body into sections: a lower shell/belt line covering the hood area with a slightly raised panel, followed by the cab section.

For the cab I'm defining door, window, and roof bands with increasing height, plus tilted boxes for the windshield to approximate the sloped A-pillars. Then I'm laying out the open-top bed section with thin wall panels and a floor, considering whether a roll bar over the bed is needed.

Rather than making windows opaque, I'm deciding to build the cab from structural pillars with open window cutouts so the driver, seat, and steering wheel are visible inside, keeping only the windshield tinted.

Actually simpler to use back-to-back cards instead. Given the part budget runs up to ~900 pieces, I want helper functions like a `box()` wrapper around part creation to keep things efficient, using cellPaint for most solid parts and reserving pixel textures for details like windshield glass, grille, license plates, headlights, gauges, and tire sidewall text.

Now I'm working out the joint hierarchy -- chassis as root, front and rear axles as hinge joints, and steering joints positioned at the kingpin locations parented to the front axle, figuring out default orientations where no explicit direction is given.

Continuing the joint definitions, I'm positioning the wheel hinges outward from the steering joints, rear wheels parenting to the rear axle, and setting up door hinges at the A-pillar with vertical axes, plus the hood hinge at the rear edge rotating about the x-axis.

Now I'm figuring out the tailgate hinge position, deciding on a bottom-hinge setup, and placing the steering wheel joint inside the cab on the driver's side with a tilted rotation axis. I'm also weighing whether to add a separate joint for a whip antenna flag or just keep the antenna rigid to stay near the 17-joint target, and starting to think through exhaust stack placement behind the cab.

For the monster truck aesthetic, I'm planning the classic chrome supercharger blower poking through a hood cutout with an intake scoop, paired with curved exhaust headers forming stack pipes for that iconic look. Then I'm sketching the chassis structure overall: box-shaped left/right rails running the length of the frame, six crossmembers spaced along the z-axis, and tube-frame front and rear bumpers made from thin rod geometry.

Now I'm adding the mechanical details underneath -- skipping the hidden engine block but including transmission and driveshaft rods connecting the front differential to the transfer case, angled up toward the axle, keeping these attached to the chassis bone for simplicity since the axle will flex independently during the random bend test.

For the axles, I'm using tube sweeps between the wheels with low-poly pumpkin diff housings (short cylinders near the front), portal gearbox boxes at each end with bolt details, and four-link control arms running from the axle up to the chassis along with a panhard bar for lateral support.

Then I'm adding chrome shock rods at each outer corner with coil springs built as spiral sweeps wrapping around them, aiming for dual shocks per side on each axle for that off-road look.

Now I'm working out the tire geometry itself—using a low-poly cylinder with faceted segments for the tread base, and considering a lathe profile to shape the sidewall curvature per wheel.

Still defining the tire profile points...

Then I orient the lathe geometry so its axis points along X and position it at the hub. I'm designing per-wheel tire paint functions that use radial distance from the hub center to create a dithered black rubber tread pattern, factoring in texture atlas costs across all four wheels.

Adding up tire tread, sidewall, and lug surface areas gives roughly 40 m² for all tires plus 40 m² for the body, totaling about 100 m² of painted surface — at a 2048px atlas that works out to roughly 5.8mm per texel, enough for the 0.04 cell size to render crisply with about 7 texels per cell, so I'll bump the atlas to 4096 for comfortable fit with gutters. Now I'm defining the lug tread blocks as chevron-patterned boxes sized roughly 0.30 axial by 0.07 radial by 0.16 tangential to mimic monster truck paddle treads.

Working out the lug layout: staggered rows around the 5m circumference with ~20 lugs per row tilted 25° into a chevron pattern, totaling around 160 boxes per wheel merged into 4 parts for about 1920 triangles. I'm then designing the beadlock steel rim as a lathed disc with an outer face, inner lip ring, and a beadlock ring carrying 20-24 small bolt boxes, colored in a chrome silver tone to sit against the tire bead.

Adding the dish, hub cap, and lug nuts now, then settling on the final color palette: hot orange body with yellow and white-ish flame highlights edged in red, black trim, gunmetal chassis with lighter edge highlights, chrome tones for the rim, and near-black tire shades.

Deciding on the accent color, I land on a teal/cyan (#19c9b8) instead of lime green for the rims, springs, shock cans, and whip flag, since orange and teal give a nice complementary contrast against the yellow flames.

Now I'm thinking through decals: maybe a number on the doors, and a playful pixel pig mascot wearing sunglasses on the hood or doors, with "MUD HOG" lettering on the bed or tailgate. I'll sketch the small pixel pig face as a compact grid before placing it, then move on to painting the body panels.

For the body color function, I'm setting up an orange shading ramp from dark to light based on surface normal direction, mimicking top-down lighting, with dithering for texture, and adding a flame graphic running along the side panels near the front.

Still designing flame geometry...

Still shaping the flame tongues...

Now I'm adding a black pixel outline around flame edges by checking neighboring cells for empty space, plus racing stripes down the hood and roof center, and thinking through door panel lines using painted outlines on the side faces.

Defining door thickness and panel outline, then laying out the body pieces layer by layer—floor pan, rocker sills, and the rest of the chassis-mounted components.

Now I'm sketching the front end: nose and fender boxes, then a separate hood panel bone sitting atop them with a cutout allowance for a possible blower, keeping fenders taller than the hood centerline for pickup-truck styling.

The blower itself should be rigid on the chassis, visible through a gap in the hood, so I'm building the hood as a frame of four strips (front, rear, two sides) around an opening rather than a solid panel, leaving space for the scoop beneath. Below that opening I'll place a dark engine block visible inside the hollow engine bay.

I'm simplifying the engine bay as a dark box with a blower above, then trying to work out the nose geometry as separate fender boxes plus a front valance, deciding whether the hood should just sit as a solid orange box over the engine or have an actual opening showing it underneath.

Now I'm sketching the layered nose: fenders on each side, a front grille panel, and a rear firewall piece, then figuring out the hood as a thin plate resting above the fenders with a rectangular cutout. I'm breaking the hood into front, rear, and side strip segments so the opening lines up correctly over the engine box.

I'm also designing the engine compartment itself—a dark block with chrome valve covers, a chrome blower case sitting on top with an intake scoop poking through the hood opening, and curved chrome header pipes sweeping out from each side of the engine and up through the hood with flared open ends.

I'll give the stack tops a gradient from chrome into a flame-like hue for flair. Then I'm designing the front grille plate with textured bars using a pixel texture, mixing black and silver with maybe a hood ornament detail.

For the bumper I'm adding a bull bar from box tubes, and placing boxy headlights into the fenders' front faces using a pixel-art lens texture with white and yellowish-gray tones. Now I'm moving on to the cab structure, starting with the lower body section spanning roughly from z -0.8 to 0.95.

I'm sizing the cab core narrower than the doors so the door shells sit flush against the fenders, with the door belt line around y 2.35 marking where solid sheet metal gives way to window openings above. Above that belt line I need visible interior details like seat backs so the cabin reads as hollow and occupied rather than solid.

Now I'm planning the roof structure: tilted A-pillar rods connecting the dash to the roof edge, vertical B-pillars and slanted C-pillars, then a roof slab with a sun-visor strip and a row of spotlight boxes mounted on a front bracket for the light bar.

For the windshield, I'm building a tilted glass slab between the A-pillars with a custom cell-based paint pattern giving it a dark blue tint with diagonal lighter glint streaks, oriented along its face normal. Then I'm adding a rear window as a glass box in the back cab wall.

I'm also planning the open side windows so the driver is visible through them, and starting to lay out the interior — seat bases and backs for the driver, plus a torso box to represent the driver's body.

Now I'm designing the driver's head and helmet: a small pixel-art skin box with a face showing a visor, topped by a white helmet with a teal stripe, scaled down to roughly 0.2 meters.

Working out the arms, steering wheel, and dashboard next: arms as simple rods reaching a blocky octagonal steering ring built from a closed polyline sweep, mounted on a tilted hinge joint near the dash, with the dashboard itself positioned as a cross-car box at the appropriate height.

I'm also adding an empty bucket seat for the passenger and sketching a visible roll cage inside the cabin -- thin dark tubes forming a main hoop behind the seats that's visible through the windows, built from a rounded polyline path.

Now I'm working out the door geometry: thin door skins with a window frame section up top, figuring out the A-pillar and B-pillar positions and how the cab's overall length constrains the door width for a regular-cab pickup layout.

Behind the door I'm planning the rear quarter panel and its small closed quarter window, plus door details like the handle, mirror, and hinge joint placement for later rotation animation.

Then I'm laying out the truck bed: side walls and floor dimensions behind the cab, a hinged tailgate with handle, stripe decals, and "MUD HOG" text, plus wheel wells to come.

I'm adding a roll bar light rack behind the cab with round light boxes, and loading the bed with cargo details—a red fuel can, jack, blue nitrogen bottles, and a tool box. For the rear I'm planning a tube bumper with tow hooks, pixel-textured taillights at the bed corners, a tiny "MUD 13" license plate on the tailgate, and considering tall exhaust stacks.

Now I'm placing twin chrome exhaust stacks behind the cab near the roll bar, flared at the top, plus a thin whip antenna off the tailgate corner with a small pixel-textured checkered flag card attached.

For the front end, I'm designing a tubular steel bumper with curved uprights, a centered winch box with cable drum and red tow hooks, a tubular bull bar, and fog lights integrated into the bumper since the roof already has a light bar. I'm skipping mud flaps since the tires sit outboard, and adding black trim strips along the belt line to flare the fender tops.

For the underside, I'm detailing frame rails with a lightening-hole texture using a dark square cell pattern, plus a transfer case, engine, four-link suspension rods, panhard bar, drag link steering rod, and tie rods using thin box-section geometry. I'll skip visible brake rotors since they're hidden inside the rims, but I'm adding hub shafts as cylinders extending into the wheel hubs.

For the wheels themselves, I'm mirroring the rim ornamentation onto the inner face too, using a loop over both sides, along with portal gear boxes sitting between the axle tube and the hub centerline.

Now I'm worried the shock absorbers at x 0.97 might collide with these portal boxes, so I need to shift their z-offsets outward, around ±0.3 from the axle, to clear them while still mounting properly to the axle tube.

Now I'm mapping out the joint hierarchy -- chassis as root, then axles front and rear, steering joints left and right, and the wheel joints underneath those, to make sure the steering rotation properly carries the hub and wheel with it.

I'm also working through wheel orientation: each wheel's bone direction points outward along the X axis depending on left or right side, which determines how the hinge rotation behaves, and I'm placing the wheel geometry parts relative to their bone origins so they sit correctly in model space.

I'm estimating total part counts to stay under budget, roughly 250 for the body and 40 across the four wheels, so I'm planning to merge small repeated elements like lugs and bolts by bone and color using a bagging helper that accumulates geometries under a shared key before flushing them into merged parts.

Writing geometry merge helpers...

Now I'm sorting out which surfaces need pixel textures versus flat painted colors—grille, headlight and taillight lenses, windshield glass, side window netting, and name decals all seem to need texture treatment.

Defining pixel glyphs for text rendering...

Still designing letter glyphs...

Finishing the pixel font glyphs, I'm now planning how to render text with a shadow offset for readability, then sizing the "13" numerals and "MUD HOG" lettering for the truck's door and bed panels based on pixel scale.

Checking widths against actual panel dimensions to pick the right texel size so the text fits the bed length, then figuring out how to orient the decal plane on each side so the lettering reads correctly from the viewer's perspective.

Right side checks out too. Now I'm positioning the bed-side decal, nudging it slightly off the surface to avoid z-fighting, and considering whether to extend the flame graphics back along the bed panel near the doors.

Since the same paint function governs flames across fender, door, and bed by position, continuity is automatic. I'm working out the color value formula, blending vertical gradients and brightness differences between top, side, and front/back surfaces for a dithered 5-color ramp.

Now I'm adding mud splatter near the bottom of the body using noise thresholds that intensify closer to the ground, giving a dried-mud brown look for monster truck realism, plus caked mud on the tire treads. I'm also considering adding flame tongues on the hood's top surface, starting from the front edge and running backward.

Writing flame generator function...

Still refining the flame color layers and outline detection...

Rethinking the flame geometry: instead of rising vertically, the hot-rod flames should sweep backward horizontally from the front wheel arch along the body side, with a baseline at the front edge and tongues of varying length spaced along the vertical axis, tapering toward their tips.

I'm adding a curl bias so the flame tongue centerline bends upward as it extends backward, shifting the sawtooth pattern using a quadratic offset based on distance, so the tongues visually curve up toward their tips along the hood sides.

For the roof, I'm keeping it black with trim, and considering whether to include a pixel-art hog decal on the doors along with a numeral, dropping the center racing stripe idea for now since the flame pattern covers the hood.

Now I'm sketching a pixel-art hog face design for the tailgate decal, roughing out a 15x13 grid for the ears, eyes, and snout while also planning a "13" circled decal for the doors and "MUD HOG" text for the bed. Designing pixel grid...

Continuing the row-by-row character count check, now working out row 6 and 7, including figuring out where to place the snout shape in the pattern.

Still working out row widths and tusk placement...

I'm now rethinking the eyes and brows for the sunglasses effect, trying to keep the pixel grid proportions consistent without overcrowding the face rows.

I'm settling on a small pink palette with dark accents for shading, and planning additional details like tire tread, rim bolts, and chrome highlights. For the driver, I'm sketching a helmeted head using a scaled skin box with a visor band across the face, sized to fit a standard pixel texture layout.

I'm designing the helmet visor with white panels and a dark blue glinting stripe, plus a teal racing suit for the driver's torso and arm rods connecting to the steering wheel. I'm deciding to skip adding a passenger or plush toy and instead keep it simple with maybe just a rear-view mirror detail, then moving on to pin down exact skin coordinate numbers.

Now I'm working out the wheel and tire geometry so the lugs and tire contact points sit flush at ground level, then setting up the frame rails with rubber mount blocks bridging the gap to the body floor, and placing the front bumper and frame horns before moving into the drivetrain layout.

For the differential pumpkins, I'm positioning them along the axle centerlines with the pinion input facing inward toward the transfer case -- front diff facing rearward, rear diff facing forward -- so the driveshaft geometry makes sense.

I'm placing connecting rods for the driveshafts running from the transfer case out to each pumpkin, then roughing in a box for the transmission/transfer case assembly tucked under the cab between the frame rails, sized to clear the rail width. I'll skip the fuel tank and muffler for now and move on to checking the steering tie rod geometry.

For the tie rod, I'm running it across the axle between the steering arms at the front axle bone. Then I'm working out the four-link suspension bars for each axle and side, with lower bars running from the axle outward to the chassis mount points and upper bars doing the same at a different height, deciding which bone each rod should be parented to since they span between axle and chassis points.

For the springs, I'm using a spiral helix function with a set center, radius, axis, turn count, and pitch to determine the coil geometry and overall height, then working out the mesh resolution—ring spacing by curvature angle and polygon sides—to estimate the triangle count for each spring.

Checking against mesh fineness thresholds, the spring edges risk triggering "too fine" warnings given their small radius and tight ring spacing, so I'm considering reducing sweep detail or switching to a coarser segmented approach, like stacking flat disc rings to approximate the coil shape.

Now I'm laying out the shock absorbers per side: two per axle, each with a reservoir body cylinder, a chrome rod section, and a surrounding spring, plus upper and lower mounting points and vertical posts for the shock tower.

I realize the diagonal brace I wanted would collide with the bed wall, so I need to reroute it—mounting the tower on a bracket that passes under the bed floor instead, extending outward from the rail to the shock position.

Now I'm setting up a flat color palette with constants for dark steel tones, near-black, and lighter steel shades to use consistently across the paint job.

Still defining color palette and tire paint logic...

I'm working out a pseudo-lettering ring using angular sectors so alternating blocks look like tread text, then layering in rubber shading that brightens toward the tread and adding mud speckle near the base. For the tread faces themselves, I'm figuring out shading based on which axis the lug surface normal dominates.

For the sidewall I'm identifying it by a strong x-axis normal, then setting up the tire lathe geometry built at the origin so it can be mirrored for left/right by translating to the hub afterward. For the tread lugs, I'm placing boxes around the circumference at a set radius, alternating two axial rows with angular offset and tilting each lug slightly to create a chevron V pattern, spacing roughly 22 lugs around the circle to fit the tangential width.

Now I'm adjusting the radial numbers so the lug tops sit exactly flush at the tire's outer radius for proper floor contact, shrinking the core radius and lug thickness so the geometry lines up precisely, and I'm beginning to lay out the lathe profile points defining the tire's cross-sectional curve.

I'm thinking through the winding order of the lathe profile points—since the lug rows need to fit within the tire's axial width and the lathe geometry's normals depend on whether the profile points go bottom-to-top or top-to-bottom, I need to get this ordering right so the faces render outward correctly.

I'm also planning the rim geometry as either a small lathe or simple cylinder shapes for each beadlock ring, and need to handle the left and right wheel mirroring so the outward-facing side is correctly oriented relative to the hub axis.

Still defining wheel geometry...

Planning a wagon-wheel pattern with 8 dark slots every 45° to break up the chrome cap, and checking that the paint grid resolution is fine enough relative to texel size for this small disc.

Now I'm sketching out the implementation structure—a helper map to bucket geometry by bone/color, and a `put` function that applies position and rotation transforms before merging geometry into that bucket, so I can assemble parts per-bone efficiently.

All geometry types indexed properly combine fine, and flat parts can use the merged geometry directly with flat shading applied. I'm setting up a texel constant and importing noise utilities, then starting to write the body paint function.

Defining an orange color ramp snapped to a 64-level palette, then working out a flame tongue function that computes a sawtooth pattern across periods with randomized length variation per tongue using a hash seed.

Testing period values for the side flame blades, I'm finding too few or too many tongues depending on spacing — trying 0.22 gives only three blades, 0.16 gives too many. I'm reconsidering whether the side flames should fan outward from the front wheel region instead, and thinking about shifting the pattern with a curl offset so the blades appear to curve upward as they move toward the back.

Now I'm defining a shared helper for evaluating the flame pattern at arbitrary coordinates so both the hood flames (in x,z) and side flames (in z,y) can reuse the same logic, clipping each blade to a visible range and allowing negative offsets for the curling effect. I'm also considering small panel/rivet lines and trim boxes for the body paint, and deciding the hood seams and roof paint details don't need extra marking beyond the existing edges.

Beyond the roof's dark high-light ramp, I'm planning out the metal paints — a steel ramp with rust speckles for the chassis, plus chrome, glass, and tire paints — and sketching cab details like chrome door handles, mirror arms with glass planes, and a windshield sun-strip decal reading "MUD HOG" rendered as a tilted banner plane aligned to the windshield's surface normal.

For the front grille, I'm planning a small textured plane with dark background, chrome horizontal bars, and a tiny center emblem, sized to fit the front fascia. I'm weighing whether to add sidewall tire lettering via decal planes versus simpler tick-mark rings since curved text is tricky, plus mud-splash paint-only decals, while reasoning that having many small separate painted parts is fine since we're well under any practical part-count limit.

I realize bagging by paint color will merge all same-colored body boxes within a bone into a single mesh, so I need a naming scheme for these merged parts while keeping doors, hood, and tailgate on their own bones separate. I'm confirming all geometry stays in model-space coordinates with zero offsets so painting and bone attachment work correctly, including wheel hubs properly parented to steering bones for the front wheels, and now starting the joint-building code beginning with the root chassis.

Setting up the axle and steering joints...

For simplicity I'll just center the kingpin at the hub, giving zero scrub. I'm defining the wheel joint as a hinge connecting the steering bone to the hub, oriented along the local X axis.

Now I'm placing the door hinges vertically at the front edges, the hood joint with a forward-pointing hinge axis, and the tailgate joint with a backward axis, reasoning through how bone roll affects each hinge's local X direction. Next I'm working out the steering wheel joint.

For the window nets, I'm deciding to use textured plane geometry standing along the frame axis, with alpha-cut textures representing a grid of black cells for the netting pattern.

Sizing it out: with a texel size around 0.02m, mesh squares could open every 4 pixels (about 8cm gaps) with 1-pixel (2cm) lines, mimicking real monster truck webbing while keeping the driver visible through the semi-open net.

Driver positioning check: placing the driver on the left side so they're visible through the door window, with the empty passenger seat on the right. Now I'm setting up the three.js imports and geometry utilities to start building the detailed model code, planning gradient-painted chrome bands for the headers.

I need to verify whether Joint is actually exported from the builder module before importing it, so let me check the exports in that file.

input.command: grep -n "^export" src/builder.ts | head -50; ls samples | head -5; ls src
